clue.text: Groovy district in an English county?

parts.note: a rut is a groove, so 'groovy' is read as 'rut'
a district or tract of land

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a hip, happening neighbourhood somewhere in provincial England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groovy' means trendy on the surface, but here it describes land full of grooves; the question mark flags the liberty. Rutland is England's smallest county.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Rutland is one English county, the smallest of them, in the East Midlands.

clue.text: Get the next round in?

parts.note: read as the pub call to buy the next set of drinks for the group
meant as a round of ammunition, loaded into the gun's chamber

explanation.surface: A pub drinker being told it is their turn to buy drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'round' in a pub is a set of drinks bought for the group; here it is a round of ammunition put into a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: To reload a gun is to put the next round of ammunition into it.

clue.text: See 20
Arrogance shown in an RC feast?

definitions.meaning: presumption, taking too much upon oneself
the Roman Catholic feast of Mary taken up into heaven, 15 August

explanation.surface: A haughty display at a Roman Catholic celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown in' makes the arrogance sound like behaviour at the feast; in fact the feast and the arrogance share one word, and the question mark admits the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Assumption can mean presumptuous arrogance, and the Assumption is a Roman Catholic feast day.

clue.text: Remove trousers — bad egg to miss a good thrashing

indicators.note: beating the letters about rearranges them

parts.note: taken letter for letter
G is the standard abbreviation for good; one G goes, leaving BADEG

explanation.surface: A schoolboy prank: a rotter debagged and then given a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: To debag is old British schoolboy slang for pulling someone's trousers off as a prank.
explanation.definitionFit: Debag means to strip someone of their trousers, bags being slang for trousers.

clue.text: Adult rabbit going outside to get drink

parts.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
a lop is a breed of rabbit with drooping ears
to cop is slang for to get or catch

explanation.surface: A grown-up rabbit hopping out of the burrow in search of refreshment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To get' looks like a link to the definition, but 'get' is COP and it sits inside the rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a sweet, fizzy alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Shock when pair climbing spotted mount

parts.note: to appal is to shock

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means read from the bottom

parts.note: as in 'as I left' = 'when I left'
in cricket a pair is two ducks, scores of 0 in both innings

explanation.surface: Horror at a couple scrambling up onto a spotted horse.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'pair' is the cricket term for being out for nought in both innings, hence two Os.
explanation.definitionFit: The Appaloosa is an American horse breed with a spotted coat.

clue.text: I'm surprised by king in Irish city

parts.note: 'Cor!' is a British exclamation of surprise
K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: Someone amazed to meet a monarch in an Irish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor!' is informal British English for 'wow!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cork is the second city of the Republic of Ireland.

clue.text: Margaret covering one with Nancy's black dressing-gown

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie over it on all sides
Nancy is a French city, so its word for black is French

parts.note: Peg is a pet form of Margaret
Roman numeral one
French for black

explanation.surface: Margaret throwing a black gown over a friend called Nancy.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy looks like a woman's name beside Margaret, but it is the city in north-east France.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word is borrowed from French, where it first meant a cape worn while combing the hair.

clue.text: In crowd Treebeard for one holds out

parts.note: a press is a crowd or throng
Treebeard is an Ent, a tree-giant in The Lord of the Rings

explanation.surface: In a crowd, a Tolkien character holds out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' marks Treebeard as an example of a class: he is one of the Ents.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to hold it out for someone to take.

clue.text: Inspector's wife visiting stormy isle

indicators.note: a storm tosses the letters of ISLE about

parts.note: taken letter for letter
standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A detective's wife paying a visit to a wild, windswept island.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Lewis is a British TV detective, formerly Morse's sergeant. The surface also suggests Lewis the Hebridean isle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis is the Oxford detective inspector of the ITV series Lewis.

clue.text: Single portion fills in snack in two sections

parts.note: a bite is a snack
a part is a portion
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single helping stuffed into a snack that is split into two halves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In two sections' looks like part of the snack's description, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bipartite means having or divided into two parts.

clue.text: Disease in which mercy a goal potentially

indicators.note: the letters could potentially become another word

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A disease whose cure might one day be a merciful aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potentially' means the letters are only a possible version of something else, which is why they get rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Acromegaly is a hormonal disease causing enlargement of the hands, feet and face.

clue.text: Kay previously called for joint

parts.note: a sound: 'kay' is how the letter K is said, so the name stands for the letter
née introduces a woman's former surname

explanation.surface: A woman named Kay who used to go by another name.
explanation.walkthrough: Kay looks like a woman's name, fitting with née, but it stands for the letter K.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the knee is one joint of many in the body.

clue.text: Austere existence is seen among cats at war with mice

indicators.note: IS is placed among the other letters
the letters of cats and mice fight and scatter

parts.note: taken letter for letter
taken letter for letter
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A spartan life is the lot of cats forever battling mice.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'is' is a link word; the second one is the IS that goes inside the jumbled cats and mice.
explanation.definitionFit: Asceticism is a life of strict self-denial.

clue.text: Singer one seen in uproarious 20 2: we must leave!

indicators.note: something seen in a show appears within it, so I is placed within the other letters
an uproar throws the letters into disorder
the letters W and E are removed

parts.note: Roman numeral one
the answer to 20/2
taken letter for letter, and removed

explanation.surface: A pop star appearing in a riotous episode of Fawlty Towers and being told to get out.
explanation.walkthrough: Add I to FAWLTY TOWERS, take away one W and the E, and rearrange the remaining eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Taylor Swift is one singer, the American pop star.

clue.text: Husband in jeopardy back in times past finds pig

indicators.note: one group of letters goes inside another
to go back is to go the way you came, so the letters are written from the far end

parts.note: 'days of yore' are times past

indicators.note: one group of letters goes inside another

parts.note: to be in jeopardy is to be at risk
standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband in danger in olden days turns up a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: The order matters: the husband goes into the jeopardy first, then that whole word turns back, then it lands inside the times past. A Yorkshire is a pig breed, not only a county.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yorkshire, or Large White, is a breed of domestic pig.

clue.text: French pop excessive American consumes for entertainment

indicators.note: to consume is to eat, and what is eaten ends up inside
the word for pop is taken in French

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top
père is French for father, and pop is a word for father
standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Over-the-top French pop music eaten up by an American audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' suggests music, fitting the entertainment theme, but it means dad, so French pop is PERE.
explanation.definitionFit: An operetta is a short light opera, a form of entertainment.

clue.text: Lock spring breaks giving uninvited access?

indicators.note: what breaks something splits it open and sits in the gap

parts.note: a lock or tress of hair
a spa is a mineral spring

explanation.surface: A lock whose spring gives way, letting a burglar in.
explanation.walkthrough: Lock and spring suggest a mechanism being forced, but a lock is hair and a spring is water.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespass is entering land or property without permission.

clue.text: Endlessly dangerous Romeo up for fun indoors

indicators.note: the last letter of PARLOUS is dropped

parts.note: parlous means dangerous; without its end it is PARLOU
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to be game is to be up for something

explanation.surface: A reckless lover keen on some fun at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dangerous' is parlous, an old word for perilous; 'up for' reads as a phrase about the Romeo but gives GAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A parlour game is a word or guessing game played indoors.

clue.text: Setter barking shows way

indicators.note: British slang for mad, so the letters go wild

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A setter dog barking to show someone the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a setter dog barking; 'barking' is British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A street is a way, as in road names like Watling Way.

clue.text: Drag queen's chasing buggy we hear in sitcom

indicators.note: FAULTY is spelt as it sounds

parts.note: buggy software is faulty
to drag or tow
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina
the S of queen's

explanation.surface: A drag queen pursuing a pushchair on the set of a comedy show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag queen' reads as one phrase but splits in two; a buggy is British for a pushchair, and in computing a buggy program is faulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Fawlty Towers is the 1970s BBC sitcom set in a hotel, starring John Cleese.

clue.text: Prickly shrub took an upward course

explanation.surface: A thorny bush climbing ever higher.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a climbing rose, so the two halves seem to describe one plant; one is a noun, the other a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose is a thorny shrub, and rose is the past tense of rise.

clue.text: Plant at least three detectives in Vauxhall?

indicators.note: the detectives go inside the car

parts.note: the Astra is a Vauxhall car model
a PI (private investigator) plus DIS (detective inspectors), so three or more

explanation.surface: Police planting a team of detectives inside a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Vauxhall is a British car maker and the Astra one of its models; 'at least three' counts one PI plus two or more DIs.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspidistra is a hardy leafy house plant.

clue.text: Map detail — it describes three main points

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it

parts.note: taken letter for letter
north, south and east are cardinal points of the compass

explanation.surface: A cartographer explaining what a small map feature shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describes' is used in its geometry sense, to draw a line round something.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small map set within a larger one, showing detail.

clue.text: Wrongdoer renouncing evil without real worth

indicators.note: to renounce something is to give it up, so the wrongdoer gives up the letters for evil

parts.note: a villain is a wrongdoer
ill means evil or harm

explanation.surface: A criminal going straight but still worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without real worth' looks like more description of the reformed wrongdoer, but it is the definition, as in 'in vain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vain means futile, lacking any real value or effect.

clue.text: Office workers' duck croaks having swallowed article

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside

parts.note: a teal is a small duck
the indefinite article
to croak is slang for to die

explanation.surface: A duck choking to death on something it ate.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea ladies once brought tea round British offices on a trolley. 'Croaks' suggests frog noise but means dies.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea ladies were women employed to serve tea to office staff.

clue.text: Principle that is absorbing Democrat completely? Almost!

indicators.note: to absorb is to soak something up and hold it within
almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: i.e. is Latin id est, that is
standard abbreviation
ALL, as in all over, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A principle that nearly wins a Democrat over completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'Almost!' look like a comment on the Democrat, but 'Almost' is an instruction acting on 'completely'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one's ideals are the principles one holds.

clue.text: Dope dealer in seconds confessed in A&E

parts.note: taken letter for letter
standard abbreviation for seconds
to sing is slang for to confess to the police

explanation.surface: A drug dealer blurting out a confession while in hospital casualty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' here is inside information, not drugs: Julian Assange of WikiLeaks dealt in leaked secrets. A&E is British hospital casualty.
explanation.definitionFit: Julian Assange published leaked secret information, dope in the slang sense.

clue.text: Grass and tree riddled with insects

parts.note: the ti is a palm-like tree of the Pacific
mothy means full of moths

explanation.surface: A lawn and a tree infested with bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The ti is a tree of Polynesia and Australasia, handy for setters; mothy means infested with moths.
explanation.definitionFit: Timothy is a meadow grass grown for hay.
